scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand it properly. The person is Jewish, but I don't think that directly affects the moral evaluation here. The main issue is about a relationship where the girlfriend is expecting the partner to handle car maintenance, specifically pumping her tire. The partner has already shown her how to do it, bought her a gauge, and explained the basics. However, she insists that he should be the one to handle it, even going so far as to say it's a man's responsibility. She also mentions that her male friends and family agree with her, which seems to reinforce traditional gender roles. The partner, on the other hand, feels that as a car owner, she should know how to do basic maintenance, especially since he's already taught her. He's also handling a lot of the household responsibilities, like cooking, cleaning, and paying the rent. He's frustrated because he's trying to encourage her to be self-sufficient, but she's resisting and relying on strangers or expecting him to do it. He offered to show her again how to use the pump, but she refused. Now he's decided not to help anymore, and he's asking if he's being unreasonable (AITA). So, the question is: Is it morally acceptable for him to refuse to pump her tire? First, I need to consider the moral principles involved here. There's the issue of fairness and equality in the relationship. He's contributing a lot financially and domestically, and he's also trying to help her with car maintenance. But she's not reciprocating by taking responsibility for her own car issues, even after being taught how. There's also the aspect of gender roles. She's insisting that it's a man's responsibility, which the partner finds outdated and unfair. He's challenging these traditional roles, which is a positive step towards equality. Another point is the practicality of her situation. If she doesn't know how to pump the tire and relies on strangers, she could be putting herself in an uncomfortable or even unsafe situation. The partner is concerned about her being stranded, which shows he cares about her well-being. He's already made an effort to teach her, provided her with tools, and even offered to help again. But she's refusing, which might indicate a lack of willingness to take responsibility. By refusing to help, he's setting a boundary, which can be a healthy way to maintain balance in the relationship. However, there's also the consideration of whether refusing to help is kind or considerate. Relationships often involve compromise and helping each other out, even when it's inconvenient. But in this case, he's already done more than his part, and she's not meeting him halfway. So, weighing these factors, it seems that his decision to refuse is a form of self-protection and a push for mutual responsibility. It's not about being mean but about establishing a fair dynamic where both partners contribute equally. Therefore, I think his action is morally acceptable because he's standing up for equality and encouraging her to be self-sufficient, which are positive values.
